title: Prague vs Budapest: Which Should You Visit?
verdict: Prague for medieval beauty and beer culture. Budapest for thermal baths, ruin bars, and more variety. Do both on the Prague-Vienna-Budapest route.

categories.name: Cost
categories.summary: Budapest is marginally cheaper. Both reward getting off the tourist trail.

categories.name: Architecture
categories.summary: Prague wins on medieval density. Budapest wins on architectural variety.

categories.name: Thermal Baths
categories.summary: Budapest has Szechenyi, Gellert, Rudas. Prague has none.

categories.name: Nightlife
categories.summary: Budapest ruin bars are uniquely unmissable. Prague has solid but generic clubs.

categories.name: Food
categories.summary: Prague wins on beer. Budapest wins on food variety.

categories.name: Day Trips
categories.summary: Cesky Krumlov is Central Europe's best day trip. Budapest's options are excellent but secondary.

categories.name: Safety
categories.summary: Both very safe. Prague has more tourist scams (avoidable). Budapest has pickpocketing on trams.

categories.name: Transit
categories.summary: Prague is more walkable. 24h pass 120 CZK vs 2500 HUF in Budapest.

faq.question: Is Prague or Budapest cheaper to visit?
faq.answer: Both are among Europe's most affordable capitals, but Budapest edges it on cost. Expect to spend around €55–75/day mid-range in Budapest versus €60–80/day in Prague. Beer in a Budapest ruin bar runs 800–1,000 HUF (€2–2.50), while Prague pub beer costs 40–60 CZK (€1.60–2.40). The biggest price difference is accommodation — Budapest has slightly cheaper options across all categories.

faq.question: Which city is better for nightlife, Prague or Budapest?
faq.answer: Budapest wins on nightlife — the ruin bars are genuinely unique experiences you won't find anywhere else in Europe. Szimpla Kert, the original ruin bar, occupies a crumbling Jewish Quarter courtyard filled with mismatched furniture, vintage art, and multiple rooms of different music. Budapest's party hostel scene is also legendary. Prague has solid clubs and bars but nothing as distinctive as Budapest's ruin bar concept.

faq.question: Are Budapest's thermal baths worth it?
faq.answer: Absolutely — Budapest's thermal baths are the city's most unique attraction and something Prague cannot offer. Széchenyi (€22–24 for a day pass, outdoor pools, Art Nouveau grandeur) is the most iconic. Gellért (€22 weekdays, stunning tile work) and Rudas (€17 for regular hours, Turkish domed architecture) each offer different experiences. Go on a weekday morning to avoid crowds. Factor in 3–4 hours minimum.

faq.question: Which city has better architecture, Prague or Budapest?
faq.answer: Prague has the edge for sheer medieval density — the Old Town, Charles Bridge, and Prague Castle complex are a concentrated architectural masterpiece. But Budapest's Parliament Building (one of the world's largest, free entry for EU citizens) and Fisherman's Bastion views across the Danube give it compelling highlights too. Prague wins on Gothic and Baroque; Budapest wins on Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau.

faq.question: What is the best time to visit Prague or Budapest?
faq.answer: April–May and September–October for both cities. Avoid July–August: summer crowds are intense and prices spike 30–50%. Budapest's Christmas markets (late November–December) at Vörösmarty Square and St. Stephen's Basilica are among Europe's best. Prague's markets are also excellent in December. Winter (Dec–Feb) is cold (–2 to 4°C) but significantly cheaper and crowd-free.

faq.question: Can I visit both Prague and Budapest in one trip?
faq.answer: Yes — they're 7 hours apart by direct train (Regiojet or ÖBB, around €20–35 one way), 1 hour by budget flight (€30–60), or 8 hours by Flixbus. A 10–12 day itinerary covering both — plus Vienna in between — is one of Central Europe's best multi-city routes. Vienna is roughly halfway, making a Prague → Vienna → Budapest routing natural.

faq.question: Which city is safer for tourists, Prague or Budapest?
faq.answer: Both are among Europe's safer cities for tourists. Prague has a documented shell-game scam problem around Old Town Square and Charles Bridge, plus occasional taxi overcharging — always use Bolt or Liftago. Budapest has fewer tourist scams but occasional pickpocketing on trams (especially Tram 2 along the Danube). Violent crime is rare in both cities.

faq.question: What are the best day trips from Prague and Budapest?
faq.answer: Prague's best day trip is Český Krumlov (3h by bus, €10 round trip) — a UNESCO-listed medieval town wrapped by the Vltava river. Kutná Hora (45 min by train, €5) has the bone-inlaid Sedlec Ossuary. From Budapest: Szentendre (45 min by HÉV train, €2.30) is a charming Danube bend town. Eger (2h by train, €8) has a castle, wine caves, and the famous 'Valley of Beautiful Women' winery district.
